heading: Headline
body: FAM should profit from the grid build-out by supplying metals, parts and repair work to the existing transformer fleet, starting with a retired-transformer recovery program at Imperial and a regional repair-and-rebuild platform, not by building transformers.

heading: Our recommendation
body:
Don't build transformers: a qualified 69-138 kV line costs $100-140M plus a test bay, above FAM's deal sizes and outside its skills. Instead, sell metals, parts and repair work into the transformers already in service (60-80M units), which is steadier than the new-plant cycle.
• Now, inside the portfolio: Imperial, Exeon and Midwest Industrial Metals recover retired transformers and factory scrap, with Transend on pickup; SFE, Metaltec, AFCO and Panther qualify with named transformer and component makers.
• One platform deal: a founder-owned regional repair-and-rewind shop (rebuilt units ship in 4-12 weeks at near-new prices), then add-ons at about 6-9x EBITDA.
• Selective add-ons where supply is still tight: radiators and heavy fabrication, aluminum castings for bushings and tap changers.
All market sizes are estimates, not current sales.

heading: Fit with Fulton's style
body:
This plan suits FAM's family-capital, metals-operator model.

Size. Each play is a lower-middle-market industrial business next to Imperial's metal flows: scrap, castings, fabrication, consumables and freight. None needs a test bay, utility type-testing or a $100M+ plant.

Permanent capital. The two lead plays depend on the existing transformer fleet (60-80M units; about 1.5-2.7M replacements a year, computed from NREL). They do not depend on the new-plant cycle. That makes them steadier, which suits holding with no planned exit. The new-plant cycle points to pad-mount overbuild in 2027-28 and mid-power loosening in 2029-30.

Check sizes (inferred from limited deal data).
• Evidence: FAM SFE Holdings raised $6.0M of equity (Form D, 2024). Mayco was bought for $31.3M (c.2012-13). Panther is about $5.4M of revenue (weak source). AFCO paid $65.5M to only 231 of its 373 ESOP participants, so AFCO was likely around $100M or more of enterprise value (inference).
• Suggested ranges:
• Projects inside existing companies: about $1-10M.
• Add-ons: about $5-30M of enterprise value.
• One platform: about $15-80M of enterprise value, co-sponsored with Ashland and/or Lorentzen and financed with bank debt plus mezzanine, as with Metaltec and AFCO.

Valuation. Pay about 6-9x EBITDA. Walk above about 9-10x on 2023-25 economics. The 12.9-14.1x paid for Prolec reflects scale, and FAM does not plan to sell, so it cannot cash in that gap. A cheap entry price only lowers risk.

Deal type. Target founder-succession and ESOP-liquidity sellers (FAM's pattern at AFCO, SFE and Metaltec), not PE auctions.

Light integration. FAM runs its companies as separate units. The cross-company links (Imperial with Transend, Metaltec, SFE and Panther) need one program coordinator and shared customer lists, not mergers.

heading: Fulton at a glance
body: Fulton Asset Management (FAM) is a Chicago family office and investment platform. It buys and builds lower-middle-market industrial businesses with permanent family capital: no fund structure and no planned exit (fultonasset.com). FAM is the investment arm of the family behind The Imperial Group, a vertically integrated Chicago metals recycling, alloying and manufacturing group founded in 1962. Imperial is headquartered at 1700 W Fulton St, which likely explains the 'Fulton' name (inference). The Aug 2025 AFCO release says FAM owns and operates 'over 20 operations', including Imperial Group, Mayco Industries, Stainless Foundry & Engineering, Metaltec Steel Abrasives, Setna iO, Panther Metalflow, Transend Logistics and AFCO Industries. FAM rarely invests alone. Its recurring co-sponsors are Ashland Capital Partners (Chicago; owns nine lower-middle-market industrial businesses) and Lorentzen Investments, with Atlas Capital Ventures listed on Mayco. The identified portfolio clusters in non-ferrous and ferrous scrap recycling (copper and aluminum wire and cable), zinc, aluminum and lead alloys and mill products, castings, steel abrasives, CNC machining and fabrication, aviation aftermarket, and 3PL trucking. None of the identified holdings makes electrical equipment or transformers.

Step 1
body: By Oct 31, 2026, name one FAM owner for the grid program and form a working group with the Imperial, Metaltec, SFE, AFCO and Transend leaders. Adopt the screens: about 6-9x EBITDA, no greenfield plants, and no business case that depends on tariffs or federal money.

heading: Step 2
body: Oct-Dec: Imperial, Exeon and Midwest Industrial Metals scope a teardown pilot. Price the equipment, confirm oil-handling and PCB permits and insurance, and approach 10-15 Midwest utilities, co-ops and municipal utilities to sign 3-5 supply agreements for retired units.

heading: Step 3
body: Oct-Nov: offer production-scrap buyback, with Transend pickup, to transformer and magnet-wire plants within trucking range: Prolec GE and Eaton in Waukesha WI, WEG in Washington MO, and Essex.

heading: Step 4
body: Nov: build a target list of 20-30 founder-owned repair and rewind shops. Make first contact with Midwest Electric Transformers (Hesston KS), T&R Electric and K P Electric. Ask Ashland and Lorentzen whether they would co-sponsor. Aim for one LOI by the end of Q1 2027.

heading: Step 5
body: Nov-Dec: Metaltec targets the blast lines starting up at PTT Raeford, Eaton Jonesville, ERMCO Waddell, JST Wytheville, Howard Ellisville, Prolec Goldsboro, VTC Rincon, HD Hyundai Montgomery and Hyosung Memphis, leading with low-carbon shot.

heading: Step 6
body: Nov-Dec: SFE and Panther send capability packages and request RFQs from Reinhausen (Humboldt TN), Trench (Charlotte NC), Hubbell PCORE (LeRoy NY), Hitachi Energy, Qualitrol and Eaton.

heading: Step 7
body: Nov-Dec: AFCO picks one plant with spare fabrication capacity and quotes enclosure sub-assemblies to Howard, Prolec Shreveport and HD Hyundai Montgomery. No capex without a purchase order.

heading: Step 8
body: Dec: Transend quotes Monterrey-to-US lanes to Prolec GE, Corefficient and Magnekon, and defines a reverse-logistics service for the teardown pilot.

heading: Step 9
body: Dec: check the radiator market. Confirm who owns Trantech, and interview VTC, WEG and Delta Star/MacLean on how much they outsource and import.

heading: Step 10
body: Q4: ask Ashland whether its precast holdings (NAPCO, Boccella) make transformer pads, vaults or substation trench, and whether a co-investment would make sense. Have Imperial Zinc list the galvanizers it supplies.

heading: Step 11
body: Track the dated signals: BLS PPI (Oct 15), Cliffs Q3 (Oct 19), GE Vernova Q3 (Oct 21-22), Korean makers' Q3 (late Oct), Hammond and Forgent (Nov), and the DOE EO rules (about Dec 24-27).

heading: Step 12
body: Early Jan 2027: hold a review to commit or cut. Fund the teardown pilot, approve or drop a repair-shop LOI, and decide whether the radiator and foundry searches continue.

heading: DOE's EO 14421 rules (about Dec 24-27, 2026) order monitoring, isolation or removal of installed Chinese bulk-power units.
body: Replacement and teardown demand rises. Speed up Plays 1-2. If instead the rules set a high MVA floor or grandfather existing suppliers broadly, the aftermarket plays are unchanged and the urgency of Plays 3-4 drops.

heading: Forgent's gross margin falls below 33%, or Hammond's below 29.5%, for two quarters; or Hammond's backlog falls a second quarter in a row (Q3 prints in Nov 2026).
body: Distribution and dry-type are softening. Keep AFCO enclosure work to contract-only, and do not approve pad-mount-related capex.

heading: At least 10 bid tabs show a median 3-phase pad-mount delivery under 20 weeks.
body: The speed premium on rebuilt pad-mounts is gone. Steer the repair platform toward substation repair and rentals, and lower the price you will pay for targets.

heading: Median substation quotes fall below 52 weeks across 10 or more 2027 awards.
body: Power-unit scarcity is ending. Slow down the radiator and component acquisitions, and pay only for 2023-25 economics.

heading: Copper drops well below about $14,500/t, or the Section 232 refined-copper schedule (15% in 2027, 30% in 2028) is changed.
body: Recalculate the teardown and scrap economics. Higher duties favor domestic secondary copper; a price collapse shrinks recycling spreads.

heading: The TJC-Sunbelt Solomon close, IPS/Belyea, Voltaris deals, or a 2027-29 sale of Central Moloney show small repair shops trading above about 9x EBITDA.
body: Switch from buying to building: open a repair and rewind shop in the Chicago area using the local winder pool, fed by Play 1 scrap.

heading: Builders announce in-house tank, radiator or enclosure lines, or buy their suppliers (as Hitachi did with Canduct).
body: Downgrade Plays 4-5 and Play 8. Focus on builders that are not integrating, such as VTC, WEG, Delta Star/MacLean and the Korean-owned US plants.

heading: The Annex III 15% tier expires on Dec 31, 2027, Section 232 part rates change, or the Jul 2027 USMCA review changes Mexican flows.
body: Import competition for radiators and castings shifts, and so do Transend's cross-border volumes. Re-underwrite Plays 3, 4 and 6.

heading: Reinhausen (Humboldt TN), Trench (Charlotte NC) or Hubbell PCORE launch local-sourcing programs or announce further expansions.
body: Speed up SFE qualification and the foundry add-on in Play 3.

heading: Welders or winders leave AFCO or acquired repair shops for new transformer plants (Howard, HD Hyundai, Hitachi Gallman; announced wages of $65-72k).
body: Budget for higher wages, or move work to Illinois and the Chicago labor pool. Slow any Southeast expansion.

heading: Construction contracts are awarded on MISO Tranche 2.1, ERCOT 765 kV or PJM 765 kV lines.
body: Start the galvanizing screen (Play 7) and Imperial Zinc's outreach to galvanizers.

heading: Cliffs offers merchant electrical-steel (GOES) allocations after 2028, and imported cores are confirmed at 50% duty.
body: Revisit a core-cutting or lamination business, which is currently on the avoid list.

heading: Avoid
body: Building or buying a transformer plant, including a 69-138 kV line. It needs about $100-140M plus a $10-20M test bay and about 2 years to win utility approval. That is above FAM's observed deal sizes and outside its skills.

heading: Avoid
body: Capex sized to pad-mount or single-phase volumes (cabinet lines, enclosure capacity) without signed orders. Pad-mount capacity is filling in 2027-28, the EO gives distribution no protection, and Chinese-owned and Korean suppliers are underbidding by 18-23%.

heading: Avoid
body: Paying scale multiples for a 'grid' label. Prolec cleared at 12.9-14.1x. Stay near 6-9x and walk away above about 9-10x on 2023-25 economics.

heading: Avoid
body: A core-cutting or lamination service center for now. Cliffs' electrical steel is not available to newcomers, imported strip reportedly pays 50% duty, and the duty on cores is unresolved.

heading: Avoid
body: Heavy haul and Schnabel rail. Both are capital-intensive and held by scale players (Barnhart, Mammoet, Bigge, Emmert, Sarens), and Transend has no such capability.

heading: Avoid
body: Test labs and field installation crews. These are service businesses outside FAM's metals-operator model.

heading: Avoid
body: Businesses that depend on dry-type transformers, which are softening (Hammond's backlog fell 6.9% QoQ), and bets on solid-state transformer startups.

heading: Avoid
body: Business cases that need tariffs or federal money. IEEPA tariffs were struck down, Section 122 was ruled invalid, the Annex III tier ends in Dec 2027, and the base case has no DPA, 48C or EDF money.

heading: Avoid
body: Auctions against PE roll-ups (TJC, IPS, Mill Point) for repair shops. Stick to proprietary succession and ESOP deals.

heading: Avoid
body: Taking retired units or used oil without PCB screening, permits and indemnities. This is a general-knowledge caution, not from the research.

heading: Avoid
body: Relying on a single vertically integrating builder, such as Hitachi, as the only customer of a component line.

heading: Avoid
body: Forcing a grid story onto Mayco, Setna iO or ZYCI.

heading: Caveats
body:
• FAM's criteria are inferred. Its size criteria, deal sizes and suggested check sizes come from thin evidence: the SFE Form D ($6.0M of equity), the Mayco price ($31.3M, c.2012-13), AFCO's ESOP payout to a subset of participants, and aggregator revenues. FAM's own website and Axial criteria could not be read.
• Portfolio coverage is incomplete. Only about 13 of FAM's 20+ operations were identified, so relevant units may be missing.
• Market sizes are estimates. All Fulton addressable-market figures (about $93-401M a year in total) estimate reachable markets, not current sales, and they overlap with each other.
• Buyer data is weak. Buyer prices and lead times are mostly weak-grade summaries of municipal minutes. No margin data was found for repair and rebuild shops.
• Target names are unverified. Named targets appear in the research as market participants; their ownership and willingness to sell were not checked.
• Some plays sit outside the research. Galvanizing and the Ashland precast idea fall outside the researched value chain. PCB and oil-handling points come from general knowledge. Ashland's holdings are not confirmed as FAM-owned.
• The picture will change soon. Everything reflects the Oct 12, 2026 deep dive, with no new web search. Q3 results, the DOE rules under EO 14421 and the question of whether cores pay 25% or 50% are all pending and could change the ranking.
